correctness.rationale: Integrating the two linear shape functions gives local mass hT/6 and inverse 2U/h; both endpoints have multiplicity two, giving B as stated. The spectrum is that of the SPD conjugate M^(1/2) B M^(1/2), not singular values of BM. Removing the short cell leaves an SPD assembled path mass and inverse-block sum, with every node still in a cell. The remaining scaled short-cell inverse contributes a rank-two positive-semidefinite term whose two positive eigenvalues after conjugation stay bounded away from zero, before multiplication by 1/ε. Min-max therefore bounds both of the two largest eigenvalues above and below by constants times 1/ε, and the remaining n−2 in a positive bounded interval (use the nullspace of the rank-two term for their upper bound). The constants are for each fixed n≥3. With two cells the two blocks share their endpoints, giving BM=((a+b)^2/4ab)I, hence no condition-number blowup even though both eigenvalues can blow up. The elementwise normalized mass eigenvalues 1/2 and 3/2 yield the uniform Jacobi bound. My separate symbolic assembly from the local basis integrals and endpoint-swap odd/even subspaces gives the displayed three-cell eigenvalues for each preconditioner. On 0<ε≤1 their ordering yields the stated spectral ratios; subtraction gives the asserted cubic over 12ε(2ε+1). The cubic decreases strictly on [0,1] and changes sign (+6 to −27), yielding the claimed direction and unique crossover. The ratio tends to 1/(6ε) to leading order. This does not imply runtime or a bound uniform in n for the divergence statement.

value.rationale: A single anomalously small cell is a natural stress test for multiplicity averaging. The two divergent modes give a matching obstruction to grading-independent condition bounds, and the minimal cycle gives a precise example in which a robust classical comparator overtakes the more elaborate method. The claim is strictly spectral, not a claim about actual solve-time ratios.
